questions.stem: You are preparing the 90-minute kick-off meeting for a project to install 400 pressure sensors across a regional water network. The charter says the aim is to cut leakage losses by 12% within two years. Your draft agenda covers the schedule, roles, reporting tools and the safety induction. Two team members have told you privately that they think the project is a routine equipment replacement. What should you change in the agenda?

options.text: Open the meeting with the leakage-reduction aim and how its success will be measured, and ask the team what that means for their part of the work.
options.rationale: A kick-off is the one moment the whole team hears the same thing at once. Starting with the aim and its measure gives every later agenda item a reason, and asking what it means for each role tests whether it has landed.

options.text: Keep the agenda as drafted and send the full charter to the team afterwards, asking everyone to read the objectives section before the first progress meeting.
options.rationale: This treats purpose as reading material rather than something the team builds together. The candidate assumes that access to the charter equals understanding of it, which the two private comments already show is not true.

options.text: Add a separate briefing for the two team members who raised it, so that the main meeting can stay focused on the schedule, roles and safety induction.
options.rationale: Two people said it aloud; others may hold the same view silently. Handling it privately treats a whole-team gap as an individual one and leaves the main meeting without the context that gives the plan its meaning.

options.text: Extend the schedule walkthrough so that each installation milestone is explained in detail, since a clear plan is what the team will use to organise its work.
options.rationale: More detail on what and when does nothing for why. A team that sees 400 installations and no leakage target will reasonably conclude it is doing equipment replacement, which is exactly the misreading to be corrected.

questions.explanation: The purpose of a project, and how success will be judged, belongs at the front of the first meeting the whole team attends, before schedule and roles. Plans tell people what to do; purpose tells them how to decide when the plan does not cover the situation. If a team can describe the deliverables but not the outcome they serve, the kick-off has not done its job however clear the schedule was.
questions.mindset: Lead with why the work exists, because everything else in a kick-off depends on it.

questions.stem: Your firm is building a two-storey extension to a secondary school that stays open throughout the work. The contract and the project's stated aim both centre on keeping pupils safe and lessons undisturbed. A groundworks subcontractor, briefed only on the drawings and programme, has scheduled piling for the fortnight of the summer exams because the rig is available then. The site manager spotted it on the look-ahead plan. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Instruct the subcontractor in writing to move the piling outside the exam fortnight, and add a clause on exam periods to its works information.
options.rationale: It fixes this clash and the next identical one, but a clause covers only what someone thought to write down. The candidate is treating a missing purpose as a missing rule, so the next unforeseen clash, such as deliveries at pupil drop-off, still happens.

options.text: Ask the school whether exams could be relocated to the sports hall for the fortnight, so the piling can proceed while the rig is still available.
options.rationale: It bends the client's core activity around the contractor's convenience, which inverts the project's stated aim. The candidate is optimising the programme instead of serving the reason the programme exists.

options.text: Hold the subcontractor to the site rules on noise and require a revised method statement showing how piling noise will be reduced during the exams.
options.rationale: Quieter piling during an exam is still piling during an exam. The candidate reaches for the nearest existing control instead of asking whether the activity belongs in that fortnight at all given what the project is for.

options.text: Move the piling outside the exam fortnight and brief the subcontractor's supervisors on why the school's operation shapes every work decision on this site.
options.rationale: The clash is resolved, and the people who plan the work now hold the reason behind the constraint. Supervisors who understand the purpose can spot the next conflict themselves rather than waiting for it to be caught on a look-ahead.

questions.explanation: Purpose has to reach the people who make day-to-day decisions, and on most projects that includes subcontractors and suppliers who were briefed only on drawings and dates. A rule tells someone what not to do in a case already foreseen; a shared purpose lets them recognise cases nobody foresaw. When a conflict reveals that a party never heard the reason for the work, fix the instance and close the gap in understanding.
questions.mindset: Pass on the reason behind a constraint, not just the constraint, to everyone who plans the work.

questions.stem: A €3m project is updating the firmware of an infusion pump. The charter lists two objectives: release before a competitor's launch in October, and pass regulatory review with no major findings. Over the last month one test lead cut a regression cycle to protect the date, while another delayed a build to add verification. Both cite the charter. Neither objective is ranked anywhere in the project documents. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Decide the ranking yourself on the grounds that regulatory approval is a precondition for any launch, and tell both test leads to apply it from now on.
options.rationale: The reasoning is attractive, but how much schedule risk to accept against review risk is a commercial judgement the sponsor owns. The candidate confuses having a sensible view with having the authority to set the project's priorities.

options.text: Require that any decision trading one objective against the other comes to you for approval, so the trade-offs are made consistently across the team.
options.rationale: It produces consistency by creating a bottleneck, and it leaves the underlying ambiguity in place. The candidate treats inconsistent decisions as a control problem when they are a clarity problem.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to state which objective takes precedence when the two conflict, then share that ranking with the team as the rule for local decisions.
options.rationale: The conflict is between business objectives, and ranking them is the sponsor's call. Once ranked and shared, every test lead can make consistent decisions without routing each one upwards.

options.text: Run a workshop with both test leads and the wider team to agree a shared view of which objective matters more when the two collide.
options.rationale: Building shared understanding is right, but the team cannot agree its way to a business priority it does not own. The candidate mistakes consensus for authority on a question that sits above the team.

questions.explanation: When a project has several objectives, a shared purpose includes knowing which one gives way when they conflict. Without a stated order, capable people will each make defensible but inconsistent choices. Ranking objectives belongs to whoever owns the business case, and the project manager's job is to obtain that ranking and turn it into a rule the team can apply without asking.
questions.mindset: Agreement on the objectives is incomplete until everyone knows which one yields first.

questions.stem: Five months into a ten-month, £1.2m project to build a consignment-tracking system for a freight depot, the team is on schedule and well motivated. The charter's purpose is to cut lost consignments by 40%. The parent company has since signed a new carrier contract that includes the carrier's own tracking service, and a three-month pilot at your depot has already cut losses by 35%. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue to the approved baseline, since the charter is still in force and the system will add tracking detail that the carrier's service does not offer.
options.rationale: A baseline authorises the work; it does not prove the work is still needed. The candidate treats an approved plan as its own justification and ignores evidence that most of the purpose has been met another way.

options.text: Rescope the remaining work to integrate with the carrier's service, using the tracking detail the team has already built to close the remaining gap in losses.
options.rationale: It may well be the eventual answer, but it rewrites the business case on the project manager's own authority. The candidate jumps to a solution before the sponsor has decided whether the purpose still warrants spending.

options.text: Brief the team on the pilot results first, so that they hear it from you, and then agree with them how to present the impact to the sponsor.
options.rationale: Openness with the team matters, but announcing a possible threat to the project before the sponsor has decided anything unsettles people over a question they cannot answer. The candidate puts team communication ahead of the decision it depends on.

options.text: Take the pilot results to the sponsor and ask whether the remaining work still serves a purpose worth its cost, setting out options from stopping to rescoping.
options.rationale: The project's reason for existing has largely been satisfied elsewhere. Putting the evidence and options in front of the sponsor keeps the decision with the person who owns the business case, while it can still save money.

questions.explanation: Keeping a shared purpose current includes asking whether the purpose still needs this project. When evidence shows the outcome is being delivered by other means, the right move is to surface it to the business-case owner with options, not to carry on because the plan is approved and not to redesign the project unilaterally. A motivated team on schedule is not evidence that the work is still worth doing.
questions.mindset: Test the work against the purpose, not just against the plan.

questions.stem: At a team day on a rail signalling upgrade, you ask the nine engineers to write one sentence saying what the project is for. Three describe meeting a new safety standard, four describe running more trains per hour, and two describe replacing obsolete equipment. The team has been delivering to plan and morale is good. What should you do next?

options.text: Run a facilitated session at the next team day to rewrite the purpose statement in words that all nine engineers can sign up to and repeat.
options.rationale: It assumes the statement is the problem before checking. If the charter already names all three aims, rewriting it fixes nothing; if it names one, the team should not be redefining the project's purpose on its own.

options.text: Re-present the charter's objectives at the next team meeting and ask each engineer to explain how their current work supports them, starting with the leads.
options.rationale: This is a reasonable remedy for a communication gap, but it assumes that is the cause. If the charter itself is ambiguous, re-presenting it simply repeats the ambiguity to a more attentive audience.

options.text: Compare the nine sentences with the charter's stated objectives to establish whether the split comes from the charter itself or from how it has been communicated.
options.rationale: The three answers may each be a fair reading of a charter that lists three aims without ranking them, or a sign that one aim was never communicated. Each cause needs a different fix, so finding which applies comes first.

options.text: Raise the split with the sponsor as a sign of misalignment and ask for a fresh statement of purpose to be issued to the whole team.
options.rationale: It escalates before the project manager knows whether anything is wrong at the sponsor's level. The candidate passes up a diagnosis that is entirely within their own reach.

questions.explanation: Divergent descriptions of purpose can come from the source document or from the way it reached people, and the remedies differ: an ambiguous source needs the owner to clarify it, while a clear source poorly communicated needs better communication. Checking the team's understanding against what was actually written is the cheap step that tells you which problem you have. Acting on the symptom alone risks fixing the wrong layer.
questions.mindset: Before correcting a misunderstanding, find out whether it started in what was said or in what was heard.

questions.stem: A housing association's sponsor has issued a vision for your hybrid repairs-service project: 'Every tenant's repair fixed right first time, at a time that suits them.' At the first retrospective, the team says the statement sounds like a slogan and asks to spend a day rewriting it in its own words. The sponsor wrote it after consulting tenants and is proud of it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Support the team's request and run a facilitated session to rewrite the vision together, then present the team's version to the sponsor for endorsement.
options.rationale: Co-creation builds ownership, which is why this is tempting. But the vision rests on tenant consultation the team was not part of, and rewriting it without tenants risks replacing their words with the team's assumptions.

options.text: Take the team's concerns to the sponsor and ask whether the statement could be revised to reflect how the people delivering the work would describe it.
options.rationale: It is respectful of authority, but it spends the sponsor's goodwill on wording when the team's real need is to connect the vision to its work. The candidate escalates a problem the project manager can address directly.

options.text: Explain the tenant consultation behind the statement to the team, and move the retrospective on to the working practices it is meant to improve.
options.rationale: The context is worth sharing, but explanation alone leaves the team as an audience for the vision. The candidate addresses the team's doubt about the source and not its need to make the purpose its own.

options.text: Keep the sponsor's statement and have the team work out what it means for their own work, then check those interpretations with the sponsor.
options.rationale: The why stays with the sponsor and the tenants behind it, while the team gains ownership by translating it into its own decisions. Checking back with the sponsor confirms the translation is faithful rather than a quiet rewrite.

questions.explanation: Ownership of a purpose does not require authorship of it. Where the reason for the work has a legitimate owner and a grounded basis, the team's route to ownership is to translate it into what it means for their own choices, which the project manager can facilitate within their own remit. Rewriting the vision moves authority to the wrong place; merely explaining it leaves the team as listeners.
questions.mindset: Help a team own a purpose by making it mean something in their work, not by changing who wrote it.

questions.stem: The product owner of a payments team writes each sprint goal as a list of the stories planned, such as 'Deliver stories 41, 44, 47 and 52.' In the last sprint two stories proved larger than expected, and the team could not tell which of the remaining ones mattered most, so it finished the easiest. As the team's agile coach, what should you suggest?

options.text: Work with the product owner to frame each sprint goal as one outcome the sprint should achieve, so the team can adjust which stories deliver it.
options.rationale: A sprint goal stated as an outcome gives the team a purpose to steer by. When work grows, it can choose the stories that still deliver the outcome rather than defaulting to the easiest.

options.text: Ask the product owner to rank the stories within each sprint, so that when work runs over the team knows which ones to finish first.
options.rationale: Ranking helps with order but still leaves the sprint defined as a list. The candidate improves the sequencing of the work without giving the team the single objective that would let it judge which stories actually matter.

options.text: Encourage the team to split stories more finely during refinement, so that size surprises are smaller and the planned list can be completed in full.
options.rationale: Smaller stories reduce the size of surprises but not their existence. The candidate treats the symptom, estimation error, and leaves the team with no shared reason to prefer one story over another.

options.text: Suggest the team commits to fewer stories per sprint, leaving enough slack that unexpected growth in one story does not put the others at risk.
options.rationale: Slack absorbs some overruns, but the team is still choosing between stories with nothing to choose by. The candidate solves for completion rather than for coherence.

questions.explanation: A sprint goal is the short-horizon expression of purpose: a single objective that the sprint's stories serve, so the team can trade scope while still succeeding. A list of stories offers no basis for that trade, and teams under pressure then optimise for ease. Framing the goal as an outcome is what turns the team from completing items into pursuing a result.
questions.mindset: Give the team an outcome to aim at, so it can choose its work when plans slip.

questions.stem: A team building a language-learning app has raised its velocity from 28 to 41 points over six sprints, and sprint reviews have become celebrations of that rise. The product goal is to lift 30-day learner retention from 22% to 30%, but retention has not moved, and the figure is only reported quarterly to the leadership team. What should the agile project manager do?

options.text: Run a retrospective focused on why retention has stalled, asking the team to identify which recent features should have moved the figure the most.
options.rationale: Inquiry is useful, but a one-off retrospective leaves the outcome invisible at every review that follows. The candidate investigates once when the problem is that the team never sees the measure it exists to move.

options.text: Arrange for the retention figure to be shown at every sprint review beside the increment, so the team and stakeholders judge progress against the goal.
options.rationale: The team celebrates velocity because velocity is what it sees. Putting the outcome measure in the review changes what progress means, and lets everyone notice that output is rising while the purpose is not being met.

options.text: Ask the product owner to reorder the backlog towards features with the strongest likely link to retention, and explain the change at the next planning.
options.rationale: Reprioritising may be right later, but without the figure in front of the team, nobody can tell whether the new order works either. The candidate changes the work before fixing what the team pays attention to.

options.text: Suggest the team stops tracking velocity at reviews, since a rising point count is drawing attention away from the outcome the product exists to deliver.
options.rationale: Removing the output measure leaves a gap without filling it with the outcome. The candidate correctly diagnoses misplaced attention but treats subtraction as if it were redirection.

questions.explanation: Teams steer by the measures they see most often. When the purpose is an outcome reported somewhere else, output measures fill the space and become the de facto goal. Keeping the outcome measure in the team's regular routines, alongside the work, is what keeps the shared purpose live and lets the team notice early when activity and results diverge.
questions.mindset: Put the measure of purpose where the team looks every week.

questions.stem: Two quarters ago a council's web team wrote a product vision promising 'accessible online services for every resident.' Since then the team has come to treat 'accessible' as meaning the recognised accessibility standard plus plain-language content tested with residents who have learning disabilities. The product owner and service users praise the results. The written vision still uses the original wording. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Leave the vision as written, since the team and its users clearly share the fuller meaning and the wording has not caused any problems so far.
options.rationale: The shared meaning lives only in the heads of the current team. The candidate mistakes present understanding for durable understanding, and the first new joiner or new product owner will read the narrower words.

options.text: Propose to the product owner that the vision is updated to state the fuller meaning the team now works to, so newcomers inherit it too.
options.rationale: The team's understanding has improved and the people who own the product endorse it. Writing it down keeps the stated purpose and the practised one aligned, and the product owner remains the one who decides the wording.

options.text: Remind the team that the vision commits only to the standard, and check that plain-language testing is not taking capacity from other committed work.
options.rationale: It treats a valued, endorsed improvement in the team's understanding as drift to be policed. The candidate holds to the letter of the purpose against an evolution that the product owner and users have welcomed.

options.text: Raise the change with the service's senior sponsor as possible scope creep, and ask for a decision on whether the extra testing should continue.
options.rationale: The product owner already owns and endorses this interpretation, so escalating it as creep second-guesses the right decision-maker. The candidate sees a change in meaning as a change in scope.

questions.explanation: A shared purpose evolves as a team learns, and that is healthy when the people who own the product endorse the change. The risk is that the written statement lags behind the practised one, so the next person to join learns the old purpose. Keeping a purpose current means capturing improved understanding through its owner, not freezing the original words or treating every evolution as drift.
questions.mindset: When the team's understanding of the purpose improves, update the words so the improvement outlasts the people.

questions.stem: Your start-up's product vision is a self-service route-planning tool for small courier firms. A large retailer has offered €180,000 for a custom integration with its warehouse system, work no other customer would use. The money would fund about four months of the team's costs, and the founders have agreed to take it. The team fears the vision is being abandoned. As the agile project manager, what should you recommend?

options.text: Update the product vision to include enterprise integrations, so that the retailer work sits within the stated purpose and the team's concern is resolved.
options.rationale: It removes the tension by redefining the purpose around a single deal. The candidate trades the long-term direction for short-term comfort, and the team now has a vision that no longer guides anything.

options.text: Present the integration to the team as a time-boxed detour that funds the vision, and keep the product goal unchanged so the team knows where it returns.
options.rationale: It names the trade-off honestly: off-vision work accepted for a reason that serves the vision. Keeping the product goal fixed and the detour bounded preserves the shared direction while the money is earned.

options.text: Ask the founders to reconsider, setting out in detail how a single-customer integration diverts the team from the self-service tool that the vision describes.
options.rationale: The founders have weighed runway against focus and decided. The candidate reopens a legitimate business decision rather than helping the team understand how it fits the purpose.

options.text: Absorb the integration into the normal backlog and prioritise it like any other item, so the team treats it as routine work rather than as a break.
options.rationale: Disguising a departure as routine is exactly what makes a team suspect the purpose has changed. The candidate hides the trade-off instead of naming it.

questions.explanation: Organisations sometimes take on work that does not serve the stated purpose, for good reasons such as funding. The shared purpose survives that if the departure is named as a deliberate, bounded trade-off and the purpose itself is left intact. It is damaged when the purpose is quietly redefined to fit the deal, or when the departure is passed off as normal work.
questions.mindset: Name a deliberate detour as a detour, so the destination stays clear.

questions.stem: You lead a hybrid project to digitise patient records at a hospital trust. The agreed purpose is to give clinicians back time spent searching for notes. At 7pm you see the communications team's draft newsletter, due to reach all 4,000 staff at 8am tomorrow, which says that under the project 'doctors and nurses will type up all their own notes'. Clinicians are the key user group for the rollout. What should you do?

options.text: Contact the communications lead tonight, explain the agreed purpose, and ask for the item to be corrected or held before tomorrow's send.
options.rationale: Once the newsletter lands, the wrong purpose becomes the one 4,000 people heard first, and clinicians will read the project as more work rather than less. A correction before sending costs one phone call; after sending it costs months of trust.

options.text: Let the newsletter go out and use the next all-staff briefing to set out the agreed purpose clearly, with clinicians describing the benefit in their own words.
options.rationale: The briefing is a good idea but arrives after the damage is done. The candidate underestimates how hard a first impression about extra workload is to reverse, especially among the user group the rollout depends on.

options.text: Email the sponsor tonight about the inaccurate framing and ask them to decide in the morning whether the communications team should issue a correction.
options.rationale: Routing to the sponsor is reasonable for contested decisions, but this is a factual error in describing an agreed purpose, and the morning decision lands after the 8am send. The candidate escalates where direct action is both possible and within role.

options.text: Meet the senior clinical leads first thing tomorrow to explain the project's real purpose before the newsletter reaches them through their inboxes.
options.rationale: Reaching clinical leads early is thoughtful, but a handful of leads seen first thing will not outpace an 8am send, and it leaves 4,000 other staff with the wrong message. The candidate manages the reaction instead of preventing the cause.

questions.explanation: A project's purpose is shaped by the first version people hear, and an inaccurate framing that reaches a whole organisation is far harder to correct than to stop. When a misstatement of an agreed purpose is about to be broadcast and you can prevent it within your role, act before it goes out rather than planning a correction afterwards. Escalation is for decisions that need someone else's authority, not for errors you can fix in time.
questions.mindset: Stop a wrong account of the purpose before it spreads, because correcting it later costs far more.

questions.stem: A charity's product team is building a monthly-giving feature. The product goal for this quarter is to learn whether 500 pilot donors will sign up and keep giving for three months. The senior developers propose spending the next two sprints re-architecting the platform so it can scale to a million users, arguing that doing it later will cost far more. What should the agile project manager do?

options.text: Support the proposal, since the developers are best placed to judge technical risk and a rebuild later would cost the charity considerably more.
options.rationale: Developer judgement on how to build is valuable, but this is a question of what the quarter is for. The candidate defers on expertise when the issue is whether the work serves the current purpose at all.

options.text: Split the capacity so that half the team re-architects the platform while the other half continues building the pilot, keeping both pieces of work moving.
options.rationale: Splitting looks balanced but halves the effort on the thing the quarter exists to learn. The candidate compromises between two pieces of work without asking whether one of them belongs in this quarter.

options.text: Ask the team how the re-architecture helps it learn whether 500 donors will keep giving, and plan the next sprints around what does.
options.rationale: The quarter's purpose is learning, and a million-user platform answers a question nobody has asked yet. Testing the proposal against the product goal lets the team reach that conclusion itself and keeps the goal as the basis for choosing work.

options.text: Refer the proposal to the product owner for a decision, setting out the cost of re-architecting now against the projected cost of doing it later.
options.rationale: The product owner may make the final call, but the analysis offered frames it as a cost comparison and leaves the team's premise unexamined. The candidate passes on the question without reconnecting it to the product goal.

questions.explanation: Work that would be sensible for a product's eventual purpose can be wasteful for its current one. When a team proposes significant effort, the first test is whether it serves the goal of this period, especially when that goal is learning whether the product is worth scaling at all. Asking the team to make that connection keeps the shared purpose as the filter for work rather than the project manager's or the developers' preferences.
questions.mindset: Judge proposed work by the purpose of this period, not the purpose you hope to reach later.

questions.stem: Your project is moving a utility company's customer service desk to an outsourced provider. The project's purpose is to cut repeat contacts by 25%. Three months into transition, repeat contacts have risen by 8%. You find the provider's agents are paid a bonus per ticket closed, and team leaders coach them to close quickly. The contract was negotiated by the procurement director. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Share the project's purpose and the repeat-contact figures with the provider's team leaders, so they can see what the transition is meant to achieve.
options.rationale: The provider's team leaders are coaching to the only goal they have been given. Showing them the purpose and the evidence gives them a reason to coach differently while the commercial fix is pursued.

options.text: Raise the conflict between the per-ticket bonus and the project's purpose with the procurement director, and ask for the contract measures to be revisited.
options.rationale: The incentive sits in a contract the project manager does not own. Putting the evidence to its owner is the only route to aligning the provider's rewards with the outcome the project exists to deliver.

options.text: Brief the provider's agents directly in a series of floor sessions, telling them to spend longer on each call to resolve issues at the first contact.
options.rationale: The agents work for the provider, and instructing them directly bypasses their management and contradicts how they are paid. The candidate addresses behaviour without the authority to change it or the incentive that drives it.

options.text: Withhold the next milestone payment until the repeat-contact rate returns to its level before transition, citing the project's agreed purpose.
options.rationale: Payment terms belong to the contract and its owner, and the provider is meeting the measures it was given. The candidate uses a commercial lever it does not hold to enforce a purpose the contract never stated.

options.text: Add the repeat-contact rate to the monthly steering report, so the governance board can track the trend and decide when to intervene.
options.rationale: Reporting makes the trend visible to governance, but it does not reach the people whose behaviour drives it or the person who owns the incentive. The candidate mistakes informing the board for acting on a known cause.

questions.explanation: A shared purpose has to extend to suppliers, and the strongest signal a supplier receives is how it is paid. When a contract rewards behaviour that works against the project's purpose, two things are needed: the supplier's people must understand the purpose, and the owner of the commercial terms must be asked to align them. Communicating without fixing the incentive asks people to act against their pay; fixing it without communicating leaves them guessing why.
questions.mindset: Check what a supplier is rewarded for, because that is the purpose it will actually pursue.

questions.stem: You are the agile project manager for a cross-functional team building a fraud-detection product at a bank. Its six members report to three functional managers who set their annual objectives: data engineers are measured on pipeline uptime, analysts on report volume, and the security specialist on audit findings closed. In planning, each member pushes the work that serves their own objectives. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Meet the three functional managers to show them the product goal and ask them to reflect each member's contribution to it in their objectives.
options.rationale: The objectives belong to the functional managers, but the project manager can and should make the case to them. Aligning what people are measured on with what the team is for removes the pull in three directions at its source.

options.text: Work with the team to make the product goal the explicit test in planning, with each member stating how proposed work moves the fraud-detection outcome.
options.rationale: How the team plans is within the project manager's remit. Making the product goal the shared test in the room gives members a common basis for choosing work while the slower objective change takes effect.

options.text: Ask human resources to replace functional objectives for team members with a single team objective tied to the product, applied across the bank.
options.rationale: A bank-wide change to the performance system is far outside the project's reach and would take far longer than the problem allows. The candidate reaches for an organisational fix when a local one is available.

options.text: Have the product owner allocate work by function, so that each member's functional objectives are met within every sprint the team delivers.
options.rationale: It accommodates the misalignment rather than resolving it, and turns a cross-functional team back into three functional queues. The candidate optimises for the members' objectives instead of the team's purpose.

options.text: Escalate to the chief information officer to request that all six members be moved under a single line manager for the life of the product.
options.rationale: Restructuring reporting lines is a large intervention for a problem the project manager has not yet tried to solve directly. The candidate escalates before using the influence and authority already available.

questions.explanation: In a matrix, people are measured by their functional managers and directed by the project, and when the two pull apart, people follow what they are measured on. The project manager can work on both sides within their own role: influence the managers who set objectives, and make the shared goal the explicit basis for decisions inside the team. Organisation-wide fixes and restructures are rarely the first response to a conflict that can be addressed through influence and team practice.
questions.mindset: Use the influence you already have on both sides of the matrix before asking the organisation to change around you.

questions.stem: A community health charity is running a hybrid project to launch a mobile screening clinic, staffed by 6 paid employees and 40 volunteers. Volunteer attendance at shifts has dropped from 90% to 65% over two months. Exit conversations show volunteers feel like 'unpaid logistics staff', and their weekly briefings cover only rotas, routes and supplies. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Open each weekly briefing with the previous week's results, such as people screened and referrals made, alongside the operational updates.
options.rationale: Volunteers give time for the outcome, and they have only been shown the logistics. Regularly linking their shifts to people screened and referred reconnects the effort with the reason they joined.

options.text: Invite two volunteer representatives into the planning sessions where changes to the clinic's routes and services are decided.
options.rationale: Including volunteers where decisions about the service are made treats them as part of the purpose rather than as labour that serves it. It also brings their knowledge of the community into those decisions.

options.text: Introduce a recognition scheme that thanks the most reliable volunteers by name each month, with a small award at the quarterly event.
options.rationale: Recognition is welcome, but it rewards attendance and leaves the feeling of being logistics staff untouched. The candidate treats a loss of meaning as a motivation problem to be solved with thanks.

options.text: Give every volunteer a handbook setting out the charity's mission, values and the health inequalities the clinic is designed to address.
options.rationale: A statement of mission is useful background, but volunteers already know why the charity exists. The candidate supplies the purpose in the abstract when the gap is seeing it in their own weekly work.

options.text: Ask the clinical lead to record a short video explaining why the clinic exists and share it through the volunteer messaging group.
options.rationale: It communicates purpose, but once and in one direction. The candidate treats purpose as a message to broadcast rather than something kept present in routines and decisions.

options.text: Reduce weekly briefings to a short written update so volunteers spend less of their own time on the logistics they find frustrating.
options.rationale: Shrinking the logistics content removes an irritant but adds nothing about the outcome. The candidate reads the complaint as being about time spent rather than about what the time is spent on.

questions.explanation: Purpose is sustained less by stating it than by connecting it to people's regular experience of the work: the results their effort produces and a voice in decisions that shape it. One-off communications and recognition schemes have their place, but they do not change a weekly routine that presents the work as tasks without outcomes. This applies with extra force to volunteers, whose only reward is the purpose itself.
questions.mindset: Keep the purpose present in people's routine, not just in documents or one-off messages.

questions.stem: On a predictive project to build a test rig for an aerospace components manufacturer, three people come to you with questions about why the project is doing what it is doing. Match each question to the document you should use first to answer it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A supplier's engineer asks why one fixture must meet a tolerance much tighter than the usual industry norm.
After a fall in orders, the steering group asks whether the project still justifies its remaining cost.
A newly appointed team lead asks which measurable objectives the project was authorised to achieve.

options.text: Requirements traceability matrix
options.rationale: The matrix links each requirement back to the business need that created it, which is exactly what explains why a single tolerance is tighter than usual.

options.text: Business case
options.rationale: Whether the project is still worth its remaining cost is the question the business case exists to answer, and changed market conditions are the reason to revisit it.

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter records the objectives and success criteria under which the project was authorised, so it is the authoritative answer to what the project was set up to achieve.

options.text: Stakeholder engagement plan
options.rationale: Not used. It describes how stakeholders will be involved, not why the project or any requirement exists. A candidate picks it because each question comes from a stakeholder.

questions.explanation: Different documents carry different layers of a project's purpose: the business case holds why the investment is worthwhile, the charter holds what the project was authorised to achieve, and traceability links each requirement back to that purpose. Choosing the right one depends on which layer the question is really about. Answering a question about worth from the charter, or about a single requirement from the business case, gives a true answer to a different question.
questions.mindset: Identify which layer of purpose a question is about before choosing where to look.

questions.stem: You are reviewing three hybrid projects in a retail bank's portfolio, each showing a different sign of weak shared purpose. Match each observation to the most likely underlying cause. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Team members can quote the vision accurately but cannot say how their own current task contributes to it.
Team members give three different accounts of the purpose, each echoing a different director's speech, though the charter states one objective clearly.
The team's account of the purpose matches the charter exactly, but the outcome it describes was delivered by another initiative last quarter.

options.text: The purpose has not been translated into what it means at the level of individual work
options.rationale: Knowing the words without seeing the link to one's own work is the signature of a purpose that was communicated but never connected to tasks.

options.text: Senior leaders are describing the purpose inconsistently to the team
options.rationale: A clear written objective combined with accounts that track individual directors points at the leaders, not the document, as the source of the divergence.

options.text: The purpose has not been revisited since the context around the project changed
options.rationale: The team understands the purpose well; the purpose itself has been overtaken. That is a currency problem, not a communication one.

options.text: The purpose was never written down in an agreed project document
options.rationale: Not used. Each observation either quotes a clear charter or a recited vision, so a missing written purpose cannot explain any of them. It is chosen by candidates who see confusion and assume nothing was documented.

questions.explanation: Weak shared purpose has several distinct causes, and each leaves a recognisable trace: words without connection to work point to missing translation, divergence that follows individual leaders points to inconsistent messaging, and accurate understanding of an outdated aim points to a purpose that was never refreshed. Each needs a different remedy, so naming the cause matters more than noticing the symptom.
questions.mindset: Read the pattern of a misunderstanding to find where it started.

questions.stem: On a hybrid project to fit heat pumps in 300 council homes, the context changes twice in one quarter. Complete each sentence with the response that fits the change. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The sponsor confirms the aim of cutting tenants' heating bills is unchanged, but a new regulation bans the planned unit type. The project manager should
After a council strategy review, the sponsor formally changes the aim to cutting carbon emissions, whatever the effect on bills. The project manager should

options.text: keep the stated purpose and work with the team to replan how it will be achieved
options.rationale: The why is intact and only the how has been closed off. Adapting the approach while holding the purpose steady tells the team the change is technical, not a change of direction.

options.text: have the charter updated and re-brief the team on what the project is now for
options.rationale: The purpose itself has changed through its owner. The team needs to hear the new aim explicitly, because choices that served lower bills may not serve lower carbon.

options.text: continue with the current plan until the next phase-gate review considers the change
options.rationale: Not used. Waiting for a gate leaves the team working towards a plan that is either banned or aimed at a superseded goal. It suits candidates who equate governance with doing nothing until a scheduled point.

questions.explanation: When circumstances change, the first question is whether the purpose has changed or only the route to it. A blocked route calls for replanning while holding the purpose steady and saying so; a changed purpose, decided by its owner, calls for updating the authorising documents and re-establishing shared understanding. Treating either as something to wait out leaves the team working to the wrong thing.
questions.mindset: Ask whether the why or the how has changed before deciding how to respond.

questions.stem: A planning department's project exists to cut the average time to decide a householder application from 18 weeks to 12 weeks. You want to show the team progress against that purpose rather than against tasks. This month's average is 15.6 weeks. Work out how far the team has come towards its target.

blanks.label: Share of the targeted reduction achieved so far, in %
blanks.rationale: The targeted reduction is 18 − 12 = 6 weeks. Achieved so far is 18 − 15.6 = 2.4 weeks. 2.4 ÷ 6 = 0.40, so 40% of the intended improvement has been delivered.

blanks.label: Further reduction still needed to reach the target, in weeks
blanks.rationale: The target is 12 weeks and the current average is 15.6 weeks, so 15.6 − 12 = 3.6 weeks of improvement remain.

questions.explanation: Progress towards a purpose is measured against the change the project exists to make, not against the starting or target value alone. Expressing the current figure as a share of the intended improvement shows the team how much of the purpose has been delivered, which a raw figure such as 15.6 weeks does not convey. The same calculation works for any outcome with a baseline and a target.
questions.mindset: Report progress as the share of the intended change achieved, so the purpose stays the yardstick.

questions.stem: An agile team building a GP surgery booking product keeps arguing in refinement: half design for receptionists managing the diary, half for patients booking from home. Each side says the other misunderstands the users' needs. The team's product vision board is shown. Select the section the team should rework first.

graphic.title: Product vision board with five sections and their current content
graphic.caption: Select a section. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between sections, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Vision — 'Make getting a GP appointment effortless'
regions.rationale: The vision is broad but both camps can honestly sign up to it. The candidate picks the top of the board on the assumption that disagreement always starts at the highest level.

regions.label: Target group — 'Healthcare users'
regions.rationale: 'Healthcare users' covers both receptionists and patients, so each camp has read it as its own users. Until the board says who the product is for, every argument about needs and features will repeat.

regions.label: Needs — 'Book, change or cancel appointments quickly'
regions.rationale: The argument shows up as a dispute about needs, which is why this is tempting. But needs belong to a user group, and they cannot be settled while the group itself is ambiguous.

regions.label: Product — 'Online booking with reminders and a diary view'
regions.rationale: The product description already reflects the split, with features for both camps. Reworking it treats the result of the ambiguity as its cause.

regions.label: Business goals — 'Cut surgery phone volume by 30%'
regions.rationale: The goal is specific and measurable, and either user group could contribute to it. The candidate looks for the most measurable section to fix rather than the vaguest one.

questions.explanation: On a vision board, each section depends on the one it serves: needs belong to a target group, and the product answers those needs. When a team repeatedly disagrees about features or needs, trace the dispute back to the earliest section that is ambiguous, because fixing a downstream section only moves the argument. A target group broad enough to cover two different users is a common hidden source of split purpose.
questions.mindset: Trace a recurring disagreement upstream to the first assumption the team does not share.

questions.stem: You are managing a nine-month project to upgrade a building society's transaction-monitoring system so that it flags suspected money laundering more accurately. Delivery is on plan, but in team meetings developers and testers have started calling the work 'box-ticking for the regulator', and test cases for rare transaction patterns are being written in a hurry. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Invite the society's financial-crime investigators to walk the team through real cases the current system missed, and the harm those cases caused to customers.
options.rationale: The team doubts the work matters, so the remedy is evidence that it does. Investigators describing real missed cases connect the rare-pattern tests to people who were harmed, which is the reason the project exists.

options.text: Remind the team that the upgrade is a regulatory requirement with a fixed deadline, so the work has to be done to a proper standard whatever their personal view of it.
options.rationale: This confirms the team's belief that the project exists only because a rule says so. The candidate relies on obligation, which secures minimum compliance, when the problem is that people cannot see why the work matters.

options.text: Add a second review step for the rare-pattern test cases, so that another tester checks and signs off every one before it is accepted into the regression suite.
options.rationale: Extra review treats the rushed test cases as a quality-control gap. The candidate fixes the visible symptom while leaving the attitude that produced it in place, so the same corner-cutting will show up elsewhere.

options.text: Ask the compliance director to send the team a note setting out what the regulator expects and the penalties the society would face if the system fell short.
options.rationale: A note about penalties frames the purpose as avoiding a fine, which is the box-ticking view in different words. The candidate reaches for senior authority when the team needs to see the people the controls protect.

questions.explanation: People commit to work when they can see who it helps and what goes wrong without it. When a team describes a project as a formality, restating the obligation or adding control steps leaves that belief untouched; the remedy is to put the team in contact with the real consequences the work exists to prevent. A purpose drawn from evidence persuades in a way that a purpose drawn from rules does not.
questions.mindset: Show people the harm their work prevents, not just the rule that requires it.

questions.stem: A city museum's €4.5m gallery refurbishment has a charter whose purpose reads 'transform the visitor experience'. At the first design review, the exhibition designers argue for immersive digital displays, the curators for more objects on show, and the learning team for dedicated space for school groups. Each group says its proposal is what 'transform' means. The museum director is the sponsor. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the three groups to work up their proposals in more detail, so that the next design review can compare them fairly on cost, feasibility and likely appeal to visitors.
options.rationale: More detail sharpens the proposals but not the yardstick. The candidate compares solutions before anyone has said what problem they are solving, so the next review restages the same argument with better drawings.

options.text: Ask the director to agree measurable success criteria for the refurbishment, such as visitor numbers, dwell time or school bookings, before the design is developed further.
options.rationale: The disagreement exists because the purpose cannot tell the proposals apart. Defining what success will look like is the sponsor's decision, and once it is made the three proposals can be judged against something other than each group's preference.

options.text: Give the curators the deciding voice on the design, since the collection is what the museum exists to show and they are the recognised experts on how to present it.
options.rationale: Expertise in the collection is not authority over the project's purpose. The candidate settles a question that belongs to the sponsor by picking the group that sounds most authoritative.

options.text: Commission visitor research on what people want from the new gallery, and use the findings to choose between the three proposals at the next design review.
options.rationale: Research tells you what visitors want, which is useful input, but the museum may be trying to achieve things visitors would not name, such as more school use. The candidate lets data stand in for the sponsor's decision about what success means.

questions.explanation: A purpose that cannot be measured cannot settle a disagreement, because every party can read its own preference into it. When competing proposals all claim to serve the same words, the gap lies in the definition of success, and closing it is the sponsor's call. The project manager's job is to get that definition stated, with how it will be measured, before design options are compared against it.
questions.mindset: If a purpose cannot tell two proposals apart, define success before choosing between them.

questions.stem: Your sponsor has commissioned a project to separate a manufacturing division's finance, HR and IT systems from the parent company's. She tells you in confidence that the board intends to sell the division, which must not be known until the sale is announced in about six months. She suggests you tell the team the purpose is 'improving the division's efficiency'. The team is asking why the work is needed. What should you do?

options.text: Use the efficiency explanation the sponsor proposed, since the need for confidentiality is legitimate and the separation will make the division more efficient in some respects.
options.rationale: It is not the real purpose, and the team will discover that when the sale is announced. The candidate treats a convenient cover story as harmless, when it costs the credibility of every statement of purpose that follows.

options.text: Agree with the sponsor a truthful account you can give the team, such as making the division able to run on its own systems, without saying why that is wanted.
options.rationale: The team needs a purpose it can work to, and a true but partial one serves that: it guides their decisions and will still stand when the sale is announced. Confidentiality limits what can be said; it does not require saying something false.

options.text: Tell the sponsor you cannot lead the team well without the real reason, and ask her to seek the board's agreement to brief the core team under a confidentiality agreement.
options.rationale: It widens the circle of insiders on a price-sensitive matter and makes the project manager's cooperation conditional on it. The candidate assumes the team needs the whole reason when an honest partial purpose would let them work well.

options.text: Tell the team that the reasons for the work are commercially confidential for now, and that the sponsor will explain the full purpose as soon as she is able to.
options.rationale: It is honest, but it leaves the team with no purpose to guide their choices for six months and signals that something significant is being hidden. The candidate withholds everything when most of the purpose could safely be shared.

questions.explanation: Confidentiality limits how much of a purpose can be shared; it does not justify sharing a false one. The usual way through is to describe what the project must achieve in terms that are true and useful for the team's decisions, while leaving out the reason behind it that cannot yet be disclosed. A cover story buys short-term comfort at the price of every later statement of purpose being doubted, and saying nothing leaves the team without direction.
questions.mindset: Say less when you must, but do not say anything untrue about why the work exists.

questions.stem: Your project is automating dispensing at a mail-order pharmacy, and its stated purpose is to eliminate dispensing errors. At the phase-one go-live celebration, the sponsor praised the team for hitting the date 'despite a few teething defects' in the reporting screens. Since then, testers have stopped logging low-severity defects in the dispensing logic, saying the sponsor clearly cares most about dates. Phase two starts in three weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Remind the testers at the next team meeting that the charter's purpose is eliminating dispensing errors, and that every defect has to be logged whatever its severity.
options.rationale: The project manager restating the charter competes with the sponsor's public praise, and teams usually believe what leaders reward over what documents say. The candidate assumes the team has forgotten the purpose when it has concluded the purpose changed.

options.text: Introduce a defect-logging measure for the test team and report it alongside schedule progress, so that thorough defect reporting is visibly valued again in phase two.
options.rationale: A counter-metric invites gaming and leaves the misread priority in place. The candidate treats a problem of meaning as a problem of incentives, adding a signal rather than correcting the one that caused the change.

options.text: Ask the test lead to explain to the testers that the sponsor's comment was about the reporting screens, and did not refer to the accuracy of the dispensing logic.
options.rationale: A second-hand interpretation of the sponsor's words carries less weight than the words themselves. The candidate tries to correct a leader's signal without involving the leader, so the testers are left choosing between two accounts.

options.text: Meet the sponsor privately, explain how the team has read his praise, and ask him to tell the team himself that error-free dispensing comes before the date.
options.rationale: The team is reading the priority from what the sponsor rewarded, so only the sponsor can correct it convincingly. Showing him the effect of his words and asking him to restate the purpose fixes the signal at its source before phase two.

questions.explanation: Teams read priorities from what leaders visibly reward more than from what documents state. When a sponsor's behaviour appears to contradict the agreed purpose, the correction has to come from the same authority, so the project manager's move is to show the sponsor the effect of the signal and ask for the priority to be restated in the sponsor's own voice. Restating the charter, or adding a counter-incentive, competes with the signal instead of correcting it.
questions.mindset: When a leader's signal and the stated purpose diverge, take the gap back to the leader who sent it.

questions.stem: A flood-defence scheme was approved to protect 1,200 homes along a river. The funding body has now cut the budget by 25%, and the sponsor has confirmed a revised first phase that protects the 900 homes at highest risk, with the rest deferred to a later bid. Since the announcement, several engineers have said the scheme 'no longer does what it was for', and two have asked to move projects. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the sponsor to put the case for the full budget to the funding body again, so the team can see that the original purpose of protecting all 1,200 homes has not been abandoned.
options.rationale: The scope has been formally revised by those entitled to decide it. The candidate reopens a settled decision to comfort the team, which signals that the new purpose is temporary and keeps people attached to the old one.

options.text: Agree the two transfer requests promptly, then rebalance the remaining work across the engineers who have chosen to stay with the revised scheme and its first phase.
options.rationale: It treats a reaction to a change in purpose as a staffing matter. The candidate loses capable people over something that could be addressed, and leaves the remaining engineers with the same doubt.

options.text: Bring the team together to set out what the revised scheme will achieve for the 900 homes, and re-plan the first phase with them around that purpose.
options.rationale: The purpose has been narrowed, not lost, and the team needs to see the narrower version clearly. Re-planning with them around it turns a decision done to them into work they shape, which is what rebuilds commitment.

options.text: Hold one-to-one conversations with each engineer to understand their individual concerns before deciding whether a message to the whole team is needed at all.
options.rationale: Listening is valuable, but the cause here is plain and shared across the team. The candidate investigates a problem that is already understood, delaying the team-wide restatement of purpose that people are waiting for.

questions.explanation: When a project's scope is reduced, its purpose is usually narrowed rather than lost, and people need to see the narrower version clearly before they can commit to it. Once the decision has been made by those entitled to make it, the project manager's job is to restate what the work will still achieve and let the team reshape the plan around it. Reopening the decision or waiting for morale to recover leaves the team attached to a purpose that no longer applies.
questions.mindset: When the scope shrinks, restate the purpose that remains rather than mourning the one that went.

questions.stem: Your team is designing a bypass for a market town, approved by the county council after public consultation to cut journey times and take lorries out of the town centre. The team's ecologist has told colleagues the town needs better buses, not a road, and has become openly sceptical in design meetings. Her environmental work is still good, but two junior engineers have started echoing her view. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Remind the whole team that the purpose was set by the council after public consultation, and that it is not open to debate inside the project team.
options.rationale: It is accurate, but it closes the discussion without understanding it. The candidate risks pushing dissent out of sight and losing any valid design concerns bundled into her objection.

options.text: Raise her objections with the sponsor, so that the council can consider whether the case for the bypass still holds against the public transport alternative she proposes.
options.rationale: It escalates before anyone knows whether she has anything the consultation did not already weigh. The candidate sends a policy preference upwards as if it were new evidence, spending the sponsor's attention on an untested concern.

options.text: Meet her privately to hear her reasoning in full, and to understand which of her concerns relate to the design and which to the decision to build the road.
options.rationale: Her objection may hold design concerns the team can act on, alongside a policy view the project cannot. Separating the two first decides what happens next: design points come into the work, and the decision itself can be explained or, if she has new evidence, raised.

options.text: Ask her to present her concerns to the whole design team, so that everyone can discuss them openly and the team can reach a shared view on the project's purpose.
options.rationale: It invites the team to re-decide a purpose that was not theirs to set, and gives the split a platform before its substance is known. The candidate confuses openness with putting the decision itself up for a vote.

questions.explanation: Dissent about a project's purpose usually mixes two things that need different responses: concerns about how the work is done, which the team can act on, and disagreement with the decision to do it, which belongs to whoever made that decision. Working out which is which comes before either closing the debate or escalating it. A respectful hearing often recovers useful input and makes the boundary of the team's choices easier to accept.
questions.mindset: Separate disagreement with the decision from concerns about the work before responding to either.

questions.stem: In year three of a four-year project to build a civic centre designed for net-zero running over a 60-year life, most of the original design team has moved on. The value-engineering proposals now reaching you mostly save build cost by swapping specified items, such as the heat-recovery system, for cheaper ones that raise running costs. Newer staff say they did not know running costs mattered. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Arrange for the original design leads to brief current staff on the whole-life reasoning behind the key specification choices.
options.rationale: Newer staff lack the reasoning, not the documents. Hearing why the choices were made from the people who made them lets them judge future trade-offs themselves rather than relying on the specification alone.

options.text: Require each value-engineering proposal to state its effect on 60-year running costs as well as on the build cost.
options.rationale: It puts the purpose into the decision that is eroding it. Proposals that trade running costs for build savings become visible as such, while genuine savings can still go ahead.

options.text: Reject any value-engineering proposal that changes a specified item, so that the original design intent is protected for the rest of the build.
options.rationale: A blanket ban protects the letter of the design while throwing away savings that do no harm. The candidate replaces judgement with a rule, which leaves the newer staff no better able to understand the purpose.

options.text: Reissue the project brief and design statement to all current staff, with the net-zero objective set out prominently on the first page.
options.rationale: The objective was already written down; what is missing is why it drives particular choices. The candidate assumes that circulating the purpose again will change how trade-offs are judged.

options.text: Ask the sponsor for authority to approve or reject every value-engineering proposal yourself until the newer staff are more experienced.
options.rationale: Centralising the decision creates a bottleneck and keeps the purpose in one person's head. The candidate treats a gap in shared understanding as a gap in authority.

questions.explanation: A purpose survives staff turnover only if the reasoning behind it travels and the decisions that could erode it are made to show their effect on it. Circulating documents or banning changes protects the letter of the design but leaves newcomers unable to weigh trade-offs for themselves. Pairing the story behind the key choices with a decision test that surfaces the purpose keeps judgement spread across the team while making erosion visible.
questions.mindset: Make the purpose show up in the decisions that could quietly erode it.

questions.stem: A predictive project is replacing the paper booking system at a council's 14 leisure centres, to cut the cost of handling bookings and make booking easier for residents. The purpose is the same for every audience, but how you express it should fit what each audience needs. Complete each sentence with the best fit. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: For the finance committee deciding whether to release the second tranche of funding, the purpose is best expressed as
For the reception staff whose daily work will change when the new system arrives, the purpose is best expressed as
For residents hearing about the change through the council's website and posters in the centres, the purpose is best expressed as

options.text: the yearly saving in booking-handling costs and when it is expected to start
options.rationale: A funding decision turns on whether the benefit justifies the money, and when it arrives. Expressing the purpose as a saving with a date gives the committee what it needs to judge the next tranche.

options.text: what their working day will look like afterwards and why the change is being made
options.rationale: Staff whose jobs change need to see what will be different for them and the reason for it. Without both, the purpose reads as something done to them rather than something they are part of.

options.text: how booking a class or a court will become quicker and easier for them
options.rationale: Residents care about their own experience of the service. The same purpose, told as an improvement they will notice, is what makes the change welcome rather than merely announced.

options.text: the list of deliverables and milestone dates in the approved project plan
options.rationale: Not used. Deliverables and dates say what the project will produce and when, not why it is worth doing. It is tempting for the finance committee, but the committee is deciding on value, not on progress.

questions.explanation: Promoting a shared purpose means expressing one purpose in the terms each audience cares about, not writing a different purpose for each. Decision-makers need the benefit and its timing, people whose work will change need to see what changes for them and why, and service users need to see what improves for them. A list of deliverables tells every audience what is being built but not why it matters.
questions.mindset: Keep one purpose, but say it in the language of whoever is listening.

questions.stem: A team building a ferry-booking app has a product vision: 'Make booking a crossing as easy as buying a train ticket.' A respected senior developer now rejects most ideas raised in refinement by saying 'that's not in the vision', including a proposal, often requested by customers, to show live vehicle-deck space. Others have stopped suggesting ideas. As the team's agile project manager, what should you do?

options.text: Ask the product owner to rule on the vehicle-deck idea directly at the next refinement session, so the team sees that ideas customers ask for can still reach the backlog.
options.rationale: It rescues one idea and leaves the misreading untouched, so the next idea meets the same objection. The candidate settles a case when the problem is the rule people are applying to every case.

options.text: Work with the product owner to show the team that the vision is meant to test whether an idea makes booking easier, not to list the features that are allowed.
options.rationale: The developer and the team share a misreading: they treat the vision as a boundary rather than a direction. Correcting how the vision is used, with the product owner who owns it, reopens the ideas the vision exists to encourage.

options.text: Propose that the team rewrites the vision with more detail about the features and journeys it covers, so that there is less room for argument about what is in scope.
options.rationale: Adding detail turns the vision into the feature list the developer already thinks it is. The candidate resolves the ambiguity in the direction of the misreading, which suppresses ideas further.

options.text: Speak to the senior developer privately about the effect his comments are having on others, and ask him to let ideas be explored before he judges them against the vision.
options.rationale: It treats the issue as one person's behaviour. The candidate misses that the rest of the team has accepted his reading of the vision, so softening his manner would leave the shared misunderstanding in place.

questions.explanation: A product vision states the outcome a product is for, and its job in refinement is to let anyone test whether an idea moves towards that outcome. When the vision is treated as a boundary listing what is allowed, it suppresses exactly the ideas that would serve it. The correction is to change how the team uses the vision, not to add detail to it or to adjudicate ideas one at a time.
questions.mindset: Use the vision as a question to ask of an idea, not a list to check it against.

questions.stem: Your team's product vision is a simple payroll service for businesses with fewer than 20 staff. In the last quarter the sales team closed three deals with firms of over 200 staff by promising features such as multi-site shift rotas, which the product owner has not agreed to build. The team learned of the deals from the customers' onboarding calls. Which two actions should the agile project manager take?

options.text: Ask the product owner to decide, with the sales director present, how the three promised features will be handled against the vision.
options.rationale: Commitments have been made to real customers, and deciding how to honour, renegotiate or decline them is a product direction call. The product owner owns it, and having sales in the room means the decision can actually be carried out.

options.text: Arrange for the product owner to take sales through the vision and roadmap, and agree how new commitments are checked before deals close.
options.rationale: The deals happened because sales was outside the shared picture of what the product is for. Bringing them into it and agreeing a check before contracts are signed stops the next set of promises.

options.text: Ask the team to estimate the three promised features, so that the cost of the commitments is known before anyone decides how to respond.
options.rationale: Estimates may help later, but starting there treats the promises as backlog items before anyone with authority has decided they should be. The candidate gathers data in place of getting the decision made.

options.text: Raise the three deals with the sponsor as a breach of the agreed vision, and ask for the sales team's commission rules to be reviewed.
options.rationale: It goes over the product owner's head and turns a gap in shared understanding into a disciplinary matter. The candidate reaches for sanctions when the cause is that sales was never brought into the vision.

options.text: Tell the team the deals are outside the vision, so they should continue with the current roadmap until sales resolves the commitments with customers.
options.rationale: It protects the team's focus but leaves customers holding promises nobody owns, and the product owner out of a decision about the product. The candidate defends the vision without anyone deciding how it applies.

questions.explanation: When people outside the team make commitments that pull a product away from its vision, two things need fixing: the decisions already made, which belong to whoever owns the product's direction, and the route by which further commitments are made. Neither is solved by the team absorbing the work quietly or by ignoring promises customers now hold. A vision is only shared if the people who sell the product are inside it too.
questions.mindset: A vision that sales has not seen will be overruled by the deals sales closes.

questions.stem: Your team is building an app for smallholder farmers. Its vision, used to raise investment, is to give farmers live crop prices. Three sprints of field interviews show farmers already get prices by radio and that their real problem is finding buyers who pay on time. The product owner is convinced the vision must change; half the team wants to finish the price features first. What should the agile project manager do?

options.text: Support the product owner in rewriting the vision around access to buyers, since the vision is hers to own, and relaunch it with the team at the next sprint planning.
options.rationale: The product owner owns how the vision is pursued, but this vision is the basis on which money was given. The candidate stretches day-to-day product authority over a change that alters what the investors are funding.

options.text: Let the team finish the price features already in progress, so that a working release exists to show the investors before the product's direction is reopened.
options.rationale: It spends further sprints on features the evidence says farmers will not use. The candidate treats work in progress as a reason to continue, when the research has already answered the question a release would test.

options.text: Run a workshop for the whole team to explore the interview findings together, so that everyone reaches a shared view of the vision before anything is proposed.
options.rationale: Alignment matters, but the team cannot decide what the product is for, and a split team asked to agree tends to entrench. The candidate seeks consensus from people who do not own the decision before those who do have seen the evidence.

options.text: Help the product owner take the interview evidence to the investors as a proposed change of vision, with what the team would build next under each option.
options.rationale: The evidence justifies changing the vision, but the investors funded the old one. Bringing them the findings and concrete options lets the change happen quickly, with the people whose commitment rests on the vision part of it.

questions.explanation: Evidence that a product's core assumption is wrong should change the vision, but a vision that others relied on when committing money or support can only be changed with them. A product owner's authority covers how the vision is pursued; reshaping what the product is for, where funding was given on that basis, needs those funders in the decision. Bringing them the evidence and options keeps the change fast without leaving them to discover it later.
questions.mindset: Change the vision when the evidence demands it, together with everyone who committed to the old one.

questions.stem: A university's agile team is building a student wellbeing app. The product owner is in meetings most of the day, and the team now waits for her answer on small choices, such as the wording on a screen or the order of menu items, which has slowed the last two sprints. She says she trusts the team but worries they will lose sight of what the app is for. As agile project manager, what should you do?

options.text: Facilitate a session in which the product owner and team turn the app's vision into a few decision principles that the team can apply to small choices itself.
