options.rationale: The product owner's worry is that the purpose lives only with her. Turning it into principles the team shares answers that worry and removes the wait, and facilitating it is squarely within the agile project manager's role.

options.text: Agree with the product owner a fixed daily slot when the team can bring all its small questions to her, so that every answer arrives within one working day.
options.rationale: It shortens the queue but keeps every small decision with one person. The candidate optimises access to the bottleneck rather than spreading the understanding that would remove it.

options.text: Ask the product owner to nominate a senior developer as her deputy for small decisions, so that the team has someone on hand who can rule on them quickly.
options.rationale: It moves the bottleneck to someone else, who will decide by personal preference unless the purpose is shared. The candidate delegates authority without passing on the reasoning that should guide it.

options.text: Suggest the team makes the small choices itself and lists them at each sprint review, where the product owner can reverse any decision she disagrees with.
options.rationale: It speeds the team up but does nothing about the product owner's concern, and invites rework when choices are reversed. The candidate grants autonomy before the team shares the basis for using it well.

questions.explanation: Teams can make good decisions without the product owner when they share the reasoning behind the vision, not just its wording. Turning the purpose into a few explicit principles lets people judge small choices for themselves and lets the product owner trust that those choices will be made consistently. Faster access to the decision-maker, or a deputy, leaves the purpose held by one person.
questions.mindset: Share the reasoning behind the purpose so that people can decide without asking.

questions.stem: You support an internal platform team that provides deployment tools to 12 product teams at an online retailer. The platform team describes its purpose as 'world-class engineering infrastructure' and is proud of its uptime. In the latest engineering survey, product teams rated the platform poorly, saying that onboarding a new service takes three weeks. The platform team believes the survey shows a lack of understanding. What should you do first?

options.text: Share the platform's uptime figures with the product teams, so that they can see the quality of service the platform team has been providing to them all year.
options.rationale: It defends the platform team's own definition of its purpose rather than testing it. The candidate assumes the users are misinformed when they may simply need something different from what is being measured.

options.text: Add a target of onboarding a new service within one week to the platform team's goals for next quarter, and track it at each of its sprint reviews.
options.rationale: It may turn out to be the right target, but it is set before anyone has understood the product teams' needs or the platform team has accepted the problem. The candidate imposes a fix ahead of the diagnosis.

options.text: Arrange for members of the platform team to interview several product teams about what they need from the platform and what slows them down.
options.rationale: The platform team has defined its purpose by its own craft, and the survey suggests that is not what its users need. Hearing the product teams directly lets the platform team rediscover its purpose from the people it exists to serve.

options.text: Ask the head of engineering to restate the platform team's purpose in terms of how quickly the product teams are able to deliver their own work.
options.rationale: A purpose handed down from above will be complied with rather than owned, especially by a team that thinks the survey is wrong. The candidate skips the step that would let the team see the gap for itself.

questions.explanation: A team whose customers are other teams can drift into defining its purpose by its own craft rather than by the outcomes it enables. When the people it serves say the work is not helping them, the first step is to let the team hear their needs directly, because a purpose discovered from customers is owned in a way that one imposed from above, or defended with internal measures, is not.
questions.mindset: Let the people you serve tell you what your purpose is for.

questions.stem: An agile team is building route-planning software for a council's refuse-collection fleet. The product exists to save £468,000 a year in fuel, and the saving starts in the first week the software is live. The team wants to use that purpose in planning. A proposed extra feature would delay go-live by 3 weeks but add a further £39,000 a year in fuel savings once live. Use a 52-week year.

blanks.label: Fuel saving forgone for each week go-live is delayed, in £
blanks.rationale: The purpose is worth £468,000 a year. Spread over 52 weeks that is 468,000 ÷ 52 = £9,000 a week, which is the value lost for every week the software is not live.

blanks.label: Weeks the extra feature must run after go-live before its saving repays the cost of the 3-week delay
blanks.rationale: A 3-week delay forgoes 3 × 9,000 = £27,000. The feature saves 39,000 ÷ 52 = £750 a week. Repaying £27,000 at £750 a week takes 27,000 ÷ 750 = 36 weeks.

questions.explanation: Expressing a purpose as value per unit of time turns it into something a team can weigh in everyday decisions. Once a week of delay has a price, any proposal that holds back the main benefit can be compared with what it adds, and the comparison often shows that releasing first and adding the extra later serves the purpose better. The same method works for any purpose whose benefit accrues over time.
questions.mindset: Put a price on a week of delay so the purpose can take part in planning decisions.

questions.stem: You are agile project manager for a new product team at a parcel carrier, formed from staff seconded from four departments. Three purpose-related problems appear in its first two months. Match each problem to the technique that best addresses it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Before the first sprint, members from each department assume that success means something different for their own department.
The team repeatedly argues over whether to ship features quickly or polish them first, and each side cites the vision in support.
The team has never met the depot staff who will use the product, and designs from its own assumptions about how they work.

options.text: A workshop in which the team and product owner agree what success will look like and how it will be measured
options.rationale: Differing assumptions about success need surfacing and settling together before work starts. Agreeing measures with the product owner turns four departmental views into one shared definition.

options.text: Trade-off sliders agreed with the product owner, ranking speed, polish and other factors for the product's current stage
options.rationale: Both sides can cite the vision because it does not say which factor matters more right now. Explicit trade-off rankings from the product owner answer that question so the argument stops recurring.

options.text: Shadowing sessions in which team members spend time with depot staff during a working shift
options.rationale: A purpose framed around users is abstract until the team has seen those users at work. Shadowing replaces assumptions with first-hand understanding of what the product is for.

options.text: A working agreement setting out the team's core hours, meeting norms and how it handles disagreement
options.rationale: Not used. A working agreement governs how the team works together, and is tempting for the recurring argument, but it decides how a disagreement is conducted, not which side the purpose supports.

questions.explanation: Problems of shared purpose come in different forms and need different tools: divergent definitions of success need a joint agreement on measures, recurring disputes where both sides cite the vision need an explicit ranking of trade-offs, and abstract understanding of users needs direct contact with them. Tools about how a team works together are valuable but do not settle what the work is for.
questions.mindset: Diagnose which part of the purpose is missing before choosing the technique to supply it.

questions.stem: A hybrid road-safety project, combining iterative app development with phased junction works, exists to cut serious injuries on a county's rural roads by a third. The team displays the monthly casualty figures on its board. After an icy winter, casualties rose sharply, and team members say the figure makes their work look pointless. They have asked for it to be removed from the board. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree to remove the casualty figure from the board and report it to the sponsor quarterly instead, so the team can focus on the delivery measures it directly controls.
options.rationale: It takes the purpose out of the team's sight and leaves it working to outputs with no visible link to why they matter. The candidate solves the morale problem by disconnecting the team from the outcome.

options.text: Keep the casualty figure on the board as it is, and remind the team at the next stand-up that the target runs over three years, so one bad winter will not decide it.
options.rationale: Reassurance helps, but the team still has nothing on the board that reflects its own work. The candidate keeps the purpose visible without giving people a way to see how they are contributing to it.

options.text: Ask the sponsor whether the target could be adjusted for weather, so that the figure on the board reflects the project's effect rather than conditions it cannot control.
options.rationale: It redefines the purpose to make the measure feel fairer, and weather adjustment invites dispute about every month's figure. The candidate changes what success means when the problem is how progress is shown.

options.text: Keep the casualty figure on the board beside measures the team directly influences, such as junctions completed and hazard reports acted on, and explain the winter's effect.
options.rationale: The casualty figure is the purpose and should stay in view, but on its own it lags and moves with the weather. Adding measures the team can move shows its contribution, and explaining the winter puts the rise in context.

questions.explanation: An outcome measure is the clearest expression of a purpose, but it often lags the work and moves with factors the team cannot control. Dropping it disconnects people from why the work exists; leaving it alone can demoralise them. The usual remedy is to pair it with leading indicators the team can move and to explain the context, so the team keeps sight of the outcome while seeing its own contribution.
questions.mindset: Keep the outcome in view, and give people a measure of their own contribution beside it.

questions.stem: A hybrid project is delivering a discharge app for a hospital trust, whose purpose is to cut readmissions caused by medication errors after discharge. The team's benefits map is shown, with the current status of each element. The app is on schedule, but readmissions in the pilot ward have not fallen, and the team believes its part is done once the app is live. Select the element the project manager should use to show the team where the purpose is breaking down.

graphic.title: Benefits map from project output to objective, with the status of each element
graphic.caption: Select an element. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between elements, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Output — app sends each discharged patient's medication list to their community pharmacy. Status: live on the pilot ward
regions.rationale: The output is delivered and working, which is why the team thinks its job is done. The candidate looks at the team's own deliverable rather than at what has to happen after it.

regions.label: Enabler — pharmacy systems receive the list automatically. Status: working at all 9 pilot pharmacies
regions.rationale: The enabler is in place everywhere, so the information is reaching the pharmacies. The candidate suspects the technology when the status shows it is not the gap.

regions.label: Business change — pharmacist phones each patient within 48 hours to check their medicines. Status: happening at 2 of 9 pharmacies
regions.rationale: This is the first element in the chain that is not happening. The app only creates value if pharmacists act on the list, so this is where the purpose breaks, and it shows the team that delivering the app is not the same as achieving the outcome.

regions.label: Benefit — fewer medication errors after discharge. Status: not yet measured
regions.rationale: The benefit is unmeasured, which is a real gap, but measuring it would only confirm what the chain already shows. The candidate picks the missing data rather than the step that is failing.

regions.label: Objective — 15% fewer readmissions from medication errors. Status: pilot ward unchanged
regions.rationale: The objective shows that something is wrong, but not where. The candidate points the team at the symptom it already knows about instead of tracing it back to the cause.

questions.explanation: A benefits map shows that a project's purpose is reached through a chain: outputs enable changes in how people work, and those changes produce the benefits. When the outcome does not arrive, trace the chain from the output forwards and find the first link that is not happening. That link is where effort belongs, and showing it to the team corrects the belief that delivering the output completes the purpose.
questions.mindset: Follow the chain from what you built to what it was for, and look for the first link that is missing.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme launching a home-battery service for an energy supplier, three questions about the project's purpose reach you in one week. Match each question to the person or body who should answer it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A team lead asks whether the year-one target of 20,000 installed batteries could be lowered to 12,000 to protect installation quality.
Developers on the agile app team ask which of two backlog items better serves the product vision for customers.
Installers on the predictive rollout team say nobody has ever explained why the service exists and ask to have it explained.

options.text: The sponsor
options.rationale: The year-one target is part of the business case that justified the programme. Changing what the programme exists to achieve is the sponsor's decision, informed by the trade-off the team lead has raised.

options.text: The product owner
options.rationale: Judging which backlog item better serves the product vision is the product owner's job. It is a question of how the purpose is pursued, not of what the purpose is.

options.text: The project manager
options.rationale: Making sure everyone working on the programme understands why it exists is a core part of the project manager's role, and it does not need anyone else's decision.

options.text: The change control board
options.rationale: Not used. It is tempting for the target question, but a change control board decides changes to the baseline within an agreed purpose. Changing the outcome the programme is for sits with the sponsor first.

questions.explanation: Questions about purpose come at different levels and belong to different people. What the project exists to achieve belongs to the sponsor who owns the business case; how a product's vision is best served belongs to the product owner; making sure the team understands the purpose is the project manager's own work. Routing each question to the right level stops purpose decisions being made by whoever happens to be asked.
questions.mindset: Ask whether a question is about what the purpose is, how it is pursued or whether people know it, then route it.

questions.stem: Four developers have joined your hybrid project, which is replacing a city's parking-permit service, after their previous product was cancelled two months before launch. They complete their tasks competently but say little in planning and skip the optional sessions with permit holders. One told you, 'We cared about the last one, and it was binned.' Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Acknowledge the cancellation openly with them, and ask what they valued in the previous product and what they learned from it.
options.rationale: Their caution comes from a loss nobody has acknowledged. Naming it and valuing what they built and learned shows respect for the commitment they gave, which makes it easier to give again.

options.text: Give them a visible share in shaping the next release, such as leading the research with permit holders for one of its features.
options.rationale: Ownership of part of the purpose builds commitment faster than being told about it. Leading the user research also puts them in front of the people the service is for.

options.text: Give them time to settle in, and revisit their engagement at the end of the current phase if it has not improved by then.
options.rationale: Withdrawal after a loss tends to harden into habit, and the phase may run for months. The candidate treats a problem of meaning as one that time alone will resolve.

options.text: Explain the governance behind this project's approval, to reassure them that it is firmly funded and unlikely to be cancelled.
options.rationale: It addresses the risk of another cancellation, which cannot be ruled out, rather than their reason to care about this work. The candidate offers security when what is missing is purpose.

options.text: Raise their low engagement with their line manager, so it can be picked up in their objectives and development conversations.
options.rationale: Their work is competent, so this frames a loss of purpose as a performance issue. The candidate hands a problem the project manager can address to someone outside the project.

questions.explanation: People who have lost a project they believed in often protect themselves by holding back from the next one. Rebuilding shared purpose with them starts by acknowledging the loss rather than talking past it, and then giving them real ownership of part of the new purpose, so that commitment grows through involvement rather than being requested. Reassurance about funding, or waiting for them to adjust, leaves the underlying caution in place.
questions.mindset: Acknowledge what people lost before asking them to care again.

questions.stem: You are running a hybrid project to introduce a common returns process across a retailer's stores in France, Germany and Poland. The English purpose statement is 'simplify returns for customers'. Two months in, the German team has removed several local return options, citing the purpose, while the French team has added new ones. Each team works from a translated version of the statement. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Ask each country lead to translate their version back into English and explain what it means to them, then compare the readings with the sponsor.
options.rationale: Opposite actions under the same purpose suggest the teams are not reading the same purpose. Back-translation and each lead's own explanation show where the meaning diverged, so the fix addresses the real cause.

options.text: Instruct the German team to restore the local options it removed until the purpose has been clarified, so that no further irreversible changes are made in the meantime.
options.rationale: It assumes the German reading is the wrong one before anyone knows. The candidate acts on the symptom first, and may reverse the team that understood the purpose as intended.

options.text: Issue a single English purpose statement to all three teams, with a note that the English wording takes precedence over any of the translated versions.
options.rationale: People still interpret an English sentence through their own language and context, so the divergence may simply move. The candidate fixes the wording without finding out where the meaning went wrong.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to rule on whether simplifying returns means fewer options or easier ones, and send that ruling to all three country teams.
options.rationale: A ruling may well be needed, but it is the second step: without knowing how each team read the statement, the ruling will itself be translated and may diverge again. The candidate settles the question before diagnosing it.

questions.explanation: When teams working from the same purpose head in opposite directions, the first question is whether they are reading the same purpose at all. Translation, jargon and local context can turn one statement into several, and the divergence only becomes clear when each group says in its own words what it believes the purpose means. Clarifying or enforcing the wording before that check risks fixing the wrong thing.
questions.mindset: Check what people understand the purpose to say before correcting what they do with it.
